title: Generic classes, methods, bounded types, wildcards, PECS rule
shortTitle: What are bounded types, wildcards, and PECS?
keyPoints: Bounded type parameters (<T extends Number>) restrict T to a specific type or its subclasses, enabling calls to methods on the bound.
Upper-bounded wildcard (? extends T) means the collection produces elements of type T or its subclasses: you can read but not write (except null).
Lower-bounded wildcard (? super T) means the collection consumes elements of type T or its superclasses: you can write T but reads return Object.
PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) is the rule for choosing the right wildcard: extends for reading, super for writing.
Unbounded wildcard (?) means unknown type: List<?> is read-only (elements come out as Object), useful for methods that do not care about element type.
Multiple bounds are possible: <T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable> means T must implement both interfaces.
The JDK uses PECS throughout: Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src).

s1_definition.oneliner: Bounded types restrict type parameters to a specific hierarchy, wildcards add flexibility with ? extends (producer/read) and ? super (consumer/write), and PECS is the rule that ties them together: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Bounded type parameter** – `<T extends Number>` restricts T to Number or its subclasses (Integer, Double, BigDecimal), allowing calls to Number methods like `doubleValue()`
- **Upper-bounded wildcard** – `? extends Account` means "some unknown subtype of Account"; you can read elements as Account but cannot add elements (the compiler does not know the exact type)
- **Lower-bounded wildcard** – `? super SavingsAccount` means "some unknown supertype of SavingsAccount"; you can add SavingsAccount but reads return Object
- **PECS** – Producer Extends (read from `? extends T`), Consumer Super (write to `? super T`); the standard guideline from Effective Java
- **Unbounded wildcard** – `?` means completely unknown type; `List<?>` is read-only with elements as Object
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, `? extends Account` is like a report that contains accounts of some specific subtype (Savings or Current). You can read accounts from the report, but you cannot file a new account into it because you do not know whether it accepts Savings or Current. `? super SavingsAccount` is like a filing drawer that accepts at least SavingsAccount (it might also accept any Account or even Object). You can file a SavingsAccount into it, but when you read something out, you only know it is some Object.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  PECS Rule: Producer Extends, Consumer Super
  =============================================

  List<? extends Account>           List<? super SavingsAccount>
  ┌────────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ PRODUCER (read from)    │        │ CONSUMER (write into)       │
  │                         │        │                             │
  │ Account acc = list.get()│        │ list.add(new Savings(...))  │
  │  -> OK (read as Account)│        │  -> OK (write Savings)      │
  │                         │        │                             │
  │ list.add(new Savings()) │        │ Savings s = list.get()      │
  │  -> COMPILE ERROR       │        │  -> COMPILE ERROR           │
  │  (cannot write)         │        │  (can only read as Object)  │
  └────────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────┘

  Collections.copy signature:
  copy(List<? super T> dest,     <-- CONSUMER: write T into dest
       List<? extends T> src)    <-- PRODUCER: read T from src
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Bounded types restrict what types can be used as generic arguments. `<T extends Number>` means T must be Number or a subclass, enabling calls to Number methods inside the generic code. Wildcards add flexibility: `? extends T` is for reading (producer), `? super T` is for writing (consumer), and `?` is for methods that do not care about the element type.

PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) is the essential rule from Effective Java for choosing the right wildcard. When a method reads elements from a collection, declare it as `? extends T` so it can accept List<SavingsAccount>, List<CurrentAccount>, or List<Account>. When a method writes elements into a collection, declare it as `? super T` so it can accept List<Account>, List<Object>, or any supertype.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh applied PECS when building the balance calculation service. The method `totalBalance(List<? extends Account> accounts)` could accept a list of any Account subtype, while `addDefaults(List<? super SavingsAccount> list)` could write defaults into any list that accepted SavingsAccount. This maximised code reuse while maintaining full type safety.

Remember one sentence: use ? extends T to read from a collection (Producer Extends) and ? super T to write into a collection (Consumer Super).
